title: Writing practice: Bats, Paper Towels and a Railroad Letter
description: Eight short writing tasks: summarize an article, judge a fair test, interpret an old letter, argue for a crossing guard, write a hallway poster, report data, explain a character change, and tell about a bell day.

stimuli.title: Article: Bats at Work
paragraphs: Bats are the only mammals that can truly fly. Many bats come out at night to hunt insects. One small bat can eat hundreds of insects in a single night, which helps protect crops and people from pests.

Other bats, called fruit bats, eat fruit and nectar. As they travel from plant to plant, they drop seeds and carry pollen, which helps new plants grow. During the day, bats rest in caves, trees, or buildings, often hanging upside down.

stimuli.title: Data table: Testing paper towels
stimuli.caption: Dev tested three paper towels by pouring 50 mL of water on each one. He measured how much water each towel soaked up.

stimuli.title: Invented source: A letter from a girl in a prairie town
paragraphs: This letter was written for this practice. It is not a real document. The writer is Clara, a girl who lives in a small town. The letter is from about the year 1885.

“Dear Cousin, the train came to our town last week. Before the train, it took four days by wagon to reach the city. Now the trip takes one day. Papa sells more wheat because the train carries it far away. The general store has new goods: oranges, cloth, and tools from distant cities. Many new families have arrived, and our school is crowded. I think our town will grow bigger.”

stimuli.title: Facts about Oak Street
stimuli.caption: Facts about the street near the school entrance.
rows: Students who cross Oak Street each morning
Cars that pass during morning arrival

stimuli.title: Scenario: A busy hallway
paragraphs: Students at your school sometimes run in the hallway between classes. The hall is narrow and has two sharp corners. Last week, two students bumped into each other at a corner. One of them dropped a box of art supplies, and markers rolled across the floor. Your class is making posters for the hallway wall.

stimuli.title: Table: Books read by Room 4
stimuli.caption: The number of books Room 4 students read each week in October.

stimuli.title: Story: Tavi’s Piano Piece
paragraphs: Tavi was going to play the piano at the school concert. For weeks she practiced every day. But on the morning of the concert, her hands shook and her stomach felt tight. “I cannot do it,” she told her brother Jonas. “Everyone will stare at me.”

Jonas sat beside her. “Play it just for me,” he said. “Only the first four notes.” Tavi pressed the keys. The notes sounded clear and calm. She played four more, and then the whole first line. “See?” Jonas said. “You already know it.”
At the concert, Tavi walked to the piano with slow steps. She looked at Jonas in the front row and began. When the last note faded, people clapped. Tavi smiled and wanted to play again.

stimuli.title: Timeline: The day the harbor bell first rang
stimuli.caption: A day in the invented town of Port Linden, in the past.
rows: Workers lifted the new bronze bell onto the harbor tower.
Mayor Odile Marsh rang the bell once.
Fishing boats returned to the harbor when they heard it.
Families gathered on the dock to celebrate.

items.stem: Write a summary of the article “Bats at Work.” Tell the main idea and two important details in your own words.

checklist: I wrote the main idea in my own words.
I included two important details.
I did not copy whole sentences.
I used connecting words such as and, also, and because.
exemplar: Task completion: states the main idea (bats help people and plants) and two accurate details.
Paraphrase: uses own wording rather than copying.
Organization: main idea first, then details.
Vocabulary: uses terms such as insects, pollen, seeds, and crops.
Accuracy: details match the article.

support.clue: Ask yourself what the big idea of both paragraphs is. Then find two details that support that idea.
support.frame: The article “Bats at Work” is mostly about how ______. One important detail is that ______. Another detail is that ______. This shows that ______.
support.model:
Mentor example about a different article. “The article ‘Busy Beavers’ is mostly about how beavers change the places where they live. One important detail is that they build dams from branches. Another detail is that the dams make ponds. This shows that beavers shape their homes.” Notice how the summary names the article and uses the writer’s own words.

Summarize your article in the same way.

facts: Bats are the only mammals that can truly fly.
Many bats eat insects, and fruit bats eat fruit and nectar.
Fruit bats spread seeds and carry pollen, which helps plants grow.

items.stem: Dev says, “Towel Z is the best because it soaked up the most water.” Do you agree? Write a claim and use evidence from the table. Tell how Dev could make the test fair.

checklist: I said whether I agree or disagree with Dev.
I used numbers from the table.
I explained whether the comparison is fair and why.
I told how to make the test fair.
I used words such as because, however, and therefore.
exemplar: Task completion: states a claim (the test is not fair, so Z cannot be called the best) and supports it with the table.
Reasoning: notes that Z is larger (20 cm by 20 cm versus 10 cm by 10 cm), so the towels need to be the same size to compare.
Evidence: may compare X and Y, which are the same size (12 mL versus 20 mL).
Science practice: proposes using the same size of sheet and the same amount of water.
Language: connectors and complex sentences.

support.clue: Compare the size column with the water column. Which towels can you compare fairly?
support.frame: I ______ with Dev because ______. The table shows that ______. This means that ______. If we compare only the towels that ______, we see that ______. To make the test fair, Dev should ______.
support.model:
Mentor example about a different test. “A student says that Plant P grew taller because it grew 15 cm, but Plant Q grew only 10 cm. I disagree with the student because Plant P had 4 weeks to grow and Plant Q had only 2 weeks. This means the test was not fair. To make it fair, the student should measure both plants after the same number of weeks.” Notice that the writer spots the difference that is not the same.

Write your claim about the paper towels in the same way.

facts: A fair test changes only one thing; other conditions stay the same.
10 cm × 10 cm = 100 square cm, and 20 cm × 20 cm = 400 square cm.
Towel Z is larger than Towels X and Y, so it can soak up more water for that reason.
Towels X and Y are the same size, and Y soaked up more water (20 mL versus 12 mL).
The test data is invented for this practice.

items.stem: How did the railroad change life in Clara’s town? Explain at least two changes and use words from the letter to show how you know.

checklist: I explained at least two changes.
I used a detail from the letter for each change.
I told how each change affected people.
I used words such as before, after, because, and as a result.
I used my own words as well as quotations.
exemplar: Task completion: explains two or more changes (faster travel, easier selling, new goods, more families) with details from the letter.
Evidence: includes specific words or numbers from the letter (four days versus one day).
Reasoning: connects each change to how it affected people’s lives.
Language: past and present contrasts with before, after, and as a result.
Interpretation: draws a reasonable conclusion about the town’s future.

support.clue: Underline the words before the train and after the train. Which details tell about travel, work, and people?
support.frame: The railroad changed Clara’s town in several ways. Before the train, ______. After the train arrived, ______. This is important because ______. Another change was that ______. Clara wrote that “______.” As a result, ______.
support.model:
Mentor example about a different change. “When the town built a bridge, life changed in several ways. Before the bridge, people crossed the river by boat. After the bridge opened, they could walk across in minutes. This is important because children could reach school faster. Another change was that more stores opened near the bridge. A woman wrote that ‘the market is always busy now.’ As a result, the town became a busier place.” Notice how the writer uses details to show the change.

Explain the changes in Clara’s town in the same way.

facts: Railroads made it faster to move people and goods between towns and cities.
Trains let farmers sell crops far away and brought new goods to towns.
Clara’s letter is invented for this practice; in the letter, travel by wagon takes four days and by train takes one day.

items.stem: Should the school ask the town for a crossing guard on Oak Street? Write your opinion and give two reasons from the facts.

checklist: I wrote yes or no.
I gave two reasons from the table.
I used numbers from the table.
I used because.
exemplar: Task completion: gives a clear opinion and two reasons supported by table facts.
Evidence: uses numbers (85 students, about 200 cars) or the lack of crosswalk signs.
Language: uses because, one reason, another reason.
Clarity: ideas are easy to follow.

support.clue: Read each row. Which facts tell you that crossing the street could be hard or unsafe?
support.frame: I think the school ______ ask for a crossing guard because ______. One reason is that ______ students cross Oak Street. Another reason is that ______.
support.model:
Mentor example about a different request. “I think the park should have more benches because many people visit. One reason is that older visitors need a place to rest. Another reason is that families like to sit while the children play.” Notice that each reason has a short explanation.

Give your opinion about the crossing guard in the same way.

facts: The table lists 85 students crossing, about 200 cars, and no crosswalk lights or signs.
The street facts are invented for this practice.

items.stem: Write the words for a hallway poster that persuades students to walk, not run. Give two reasons and end by telling students what to do.

checklist: I wrote a clear message that tells students what to do.
I gave two reasons.
I used details from the scenario.
I used words such as because, so, and please.
I ended with a sentence that tells students what to do.
exemplar: Task completion: states the message (walk in the hallway) and supports it with two reasons from the scenario (narrow hall, sharp corners, collisions, dropped supplies).
Language: uses persuasive and polite request phrases (please, remember to).
Format: a short heading, reasons, and a final call to action suited to a poster.
Reasoning: connects each reason to safety or to keeping the hall tidy.
Audience: friendly, clear tone for classmates.

support.clue: Find two details in the scenario that show why running in the hall is a problem. What could happen at a corner?
support.frame: Please walk in the hallway! One reason is that ______. Another reason is that ______. If we ______, then ______. So please ______.
support.model:
Mentor example about a different poster. “Please use the recycling bin! One reason is that old paper can be made into new paper. Another reason is that bins keep our schoolyard clean. If we all use the bin, then fewer papers blow around the yard. So please put your paper in the blue bin.” Notice the reasons and the final request.

Write your poster words in the same way.

facts: Old paper can be recycled into new paper (used in the mentor example only).

items.stem: Write a short report that tells what the table shows about the books Room 4 read in October. Include the total, the week with the most books, and the week with the fewest.

checklist: I told what the table is about.
I wrote the total for all four weeks.
I named the week with the most books and the week with the fewest.
I used numbers from the table.
exemplar: Task completion: states the topic, the total of 80 books, the greatest week (Week 4, 25) and the least week (Week 3, 15).
Math accuracy: 18 + 22 + 15 + 25 = 80.
Language: uses comparative and superlative forms (the most, the fewest, more than).
Organization: introduces the data and reports it in a logical order.
Vocabulary: total, altogether, most, fewest.

support.clue: Add the four numbers for the total. Then find the largest number and the smallest number and see which week each belongs to.
support.frame: This table shows ______. In October, Room 4 read ______ books altogether. The most books were read in ______, with ______ books. The fewest were read in ______, with ______ books.
support.model:
Mentor example about a different table. “This table shows the number of plants sold at a sale each day. The sale sold 30 plants altogether. The most plants were sold on Saturday, with 14 plants. The fewest were sold on Thursday, with 4 plants.” Notice how the writer names the greatest and least numbers.

Write your report in the same way.

facts: The greatest number is 25 in Week 4; the least is 15 in Week 3.

items.stem: Explain how Tavi changes from the beginning to the end of the story. Tell what Jonas did that helped her change, and use details from the story.

checklist: I told how Tavi felt at the beginning.
I told how she felt at the end.
I explained what Jonas did to help.
I used details from the story.
I used words such as because, so, and as a result.
exemplar: Task completion: describes Tavi’s change from nervous to confident and happy, and links it to Jonas’s help.
Evidence: includes specific details (hands shook, played four notes, looked at Jonas, wanted to play again).
Reasoning: explains cause and effect between Jonas’s actions and Tavi’s feelings.
Language: complex sentences and connectors such as because, so, and as a result.
Organization: before, cause of change, and after.

support.clue: Find three details that show how Tavi feels at the start, and three that show how she feels at the end. What happens in the middle to cause the change?
support.frame: At the beginning of the story, Tavi felt ______ because ______. The story says that ______. Then Jonas ______, which helped Tavi ______. As a result, ______. By the end of the story, Tavi felt ______. The story shows this when ______.
support.model:
Mentor example about a different story. “At the beginning of the story, Ana felt excited about her tall block tower because she had built it all morning. The story says that she held her breath and smiled. Then her little brother ran by, which knocked it down. As a result, Ana felt angry. By the end of the story, Ana felt calm. The story shows this when she took a deep breath and began to build again.” Notice that the writer links a cause to a change.

Explain Tavi’s change in the same way.

items.stem: You are a reporter for the Port Linden newspaper. Write a short news story about the day the harbor bell first rang. Tell what happened in order and why the bell mattered to the town.

checklist: I told the events in the order they happened.
I used time words such as in the morning, at noon, and in the evening.
I used past-tense verbs.
I told why the bell mattered.
I wrote like a reporter for the town.
exemplar: Task completion: reports all four parts of the day in order and includes a reason the bell mattered (for example, boats could hear when to come home).
Language: past-tense verbs and time expressions.
Organization: logical sequence with an opening sentence that names the main event.
Development: includes details such as names and places from the timeline.
Voice: reads like a short news report.

support.clue: Find the four parts of the day on the timeline. What happened because of the bell’s sound in the afternoon?
support.frame: Yesterday in Port Linden, the new harbor bell rang for the first time. In the morning, ______. At noon, ______. In the afternoon, ______. In the evening, ______. The bell is important to the town because ______.
support.model:
Mentor example about a different event. “Yesterday in Green Valley, a new library opened its doors. In the morning, workers put the last books on the shelves. At noon, the librarian cut a ribbon. In the afternoon, children chose their first books. In the evening, families listened to a story. The library is important to the town because everyone can borrow books for free.” Notice the time words and the past-tense verbs.

Write your news story in the same way.

facts: Port Linden, the bell, and Mayor Odile Marsh are invented for this practice.
Bells and other sounds were used in harbors to send signals to boats.
